Use the nonrelativistic Newtonian spacetime $I\times E$, where $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ is an open interval with absolute time $t$ in seconds. Here $E$ is a three-dimensional oriented Euclidean affine space: its translation vectors form an oriented Euclidean vector space, but no origin in $E$ is distinguished. A **Cartesian inertial chart** is an event-coordinate map $(t,X)\mapsto(t,x_t(X))$, where $b:E\to\mathbb R^3$ is an orientation-preserving affine isometry, $w\in\mathbb R^3$ is constant, and $x_t(X)=b(X)+tw$ for $t\in I$. The affine map $b$ is auxiliary data defined on $E$, so this formula requires no evaluation at time $0$ when $0\notin I$. Each fixed-time spatial map is an orientation-preserving affine isometry with fixed spatial orientation; the spatial origin has constant velocity. Spatial coordinates are measured in metres and $w$ in metres per second. A chart may also use a translated absolute-time coordinate; at corresponding events the inertial-chart transformations are the ones displayed below. Write $\mathrm{SO}(3)=\{Q\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:Q^TQ=I_3,\det Q=1\}$. Inertial charts are related by

$$t^*=t+t_0,\qquad x^*=Qx+vt+a,$$

where $t_0$ is a constant time translation in seconds, $Q\in\mathrm{SO}(3)$ is constant, $v\in\mathbb R^3$ is a constant relative velocity in m s$^{-1}$, and $a\in\mathbb R^3$ is a constant spatial translation in metres. A **worldline** is a curve $t\mapsto(t,x(t))$ with $x\in C^2(I,\mathbb R^3)$, parameterized by absolute time; this model imposes no relativistic speed or causal condition. A **rigid observer change** is the more general coordinate change $t^*=t,\ x^*=Q(t)x+c(t)$, with $Q\in C^2(I,\mathrm{SO}(3))$ and $c\in C^2(I,\mathbb R^3)$ in metres; it is not called inertial unless $Q$ is constant and $c$ is affine in time. A frame here means an adapted Cartesian chart, not an observer congruence or a basis field.

For the initial-chart material-motion convention below, require $0\in I$. Let $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded open reference body whose boundary is locally the graph of a $C^1$ function, with $B$ lying on one side of each such graph. Identify the reference coordinates with the chosen initial Cartesian chart, and let $U$ be an open neighborhood of $\overline B$. A **material motion** is a map $\chi\in C^2(I\times U,\mathbb R^3)$ such that each $\chi_t=\chi(t,\cdot)$ is a bijection from $U$ onto an open image, has a $C^2$ inverse, and has positive Jacobian determinant; in the initial chart set $\chi(0,a)=a$. The label $a\in U$ and position $x=\chi(t,a)$ are measured in metres. Write

$$F(t,a)=D_a\chi(t,a),\qquad J(t,a)=\det F(t,a)>0,\qquad A(t,x)=\chi_t^{-1}(x),\qquad \Omega_t=\chi_t(B).$$

Here $F$ and $J$ are dimensionless and $A$ has units metres. The material map $\chi$ describes motion of the medium; it is not a change of observer or frame. The Eulerian velocity is the vector field defined by $u(t,\chi(t,a))=\partial_t\chi(t,a)$, measured in m s$^{-1}$. For a differentiable scalar or component field $f$, its material derivative is $D_tf=\partial_tf+u\cdot\nabla f$. Set $L_{ij}=\partial_j u_i$, $D=(L+L^T)/2$, $W=(L-L^T)/2$, $\theta=\operatorname{tr}D=\operatorname{div}u$, and $D_0=D-(\theta/3)I_3$; $L,D,W,\theta,D_0$ have units s$^{-1}$. Define vorticity by

$$\operatorname{curl}u=(\partial_yu_z-\partial_zu_y,\ \partial_zu_x-\partial_xu_z,\ \partial_xu_y-\partial_yu_x),$$

also in s$^{-1}$. In this library, a motion is **material-incompressible** on a region when $\operatorname{div}u=0$ there; **spatially homogeneous density** means $\nabla\rho=0$ there. These are distinct conditions. A **pathline** is a $C^1$ curve $X$ on an interval where the field is defined and the solution exists, satisfying $dX/dt=u(t,X(t))$. A **streamline at time $t_0$** is a $C^1$ integral curve satisfying $dX/ds=u(t_0,X(s))$ for a frozen $t_0$, with curve parameter $s$ measured in seconds. These are different constructions for an unsteady field.

A spatial vector is an element of the Euclidean translation space; its components rotate by $Q$ under a rigid observer change. A spatial second-order tensor is a linear map from that vector space to itself, represented by a $3\times3$ matrix in a Cartesian orthonormal basis; it transforms as $S^*=QSQ^T$. A tensor-valued constitutive response is **objective** when its values at corresponding events satisfy this transformation rule for every $C^2$ rigid observer change. For a stress tensor $\sigma$, use the tension-positive convention in which the traction (force per unit current area) on a surface with outward unit normal $n$ is $\sigma n$. Set $(\operatorname{div}\sigma)_i=\partial_j\sigma_{ij}$; the tensor contraction is $S:T=\sum_{i,j}S_{ij}T_{ij}$. Stress and traction have units Pa $=\mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}=\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$.

Within a specified model, a **primitive quantity** is a quantity adopted as input rather than constructed from the other data of that model; a **derived quantity** is assigned by an explicit construction from stated inputs and results. This status is framework-local and is independent of whether its SI unit is base or derived. In the continuum model used on this page, $\rho_0(a)$ is a reference mass-density field in kg m$^{-3}$, $b(t,x)$ is an adopted body-acceleration field in m s$^{-2}$, $e(t,x)$ is specific internal energy (energy per unit mass) in J kg$^{-1}=\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}$, $T(t,x)>0$ is temperature in K, $s(t,x)$ is specific entropy in J kg$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$, $q(t,x)$ is heat flux (heat-transfer rate per unit area) in W m$^{-2}$, and $r(t,x)$ is specific heat supply (power per unit mass) in W kg$^{-1}$. Their adoption is a physical-model choice, not a consequence of the SI. The current mass density $\rho(t,x)$ means mass per unit current volume and has units kg m$^{-3}$; for a mass-conserving motion, its construction from $\rho_0$ and $\chi$ is established from the stated balance hypotheses in the theorem on this page. A pressure $p$ is a scalar in Pa whose role depends on the selected constitutive branch. The shear and bulk dynamic-viscosity parameters $\mu,\zeta$, when that branch is adopted, have units Pa s $=\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-1}}$; thermal conductivity $\kappa_T$ has units W m$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$. The gradient $\nabla$ has units m$^{-1}$. Thus the metre, kilogram, second, and kelvin are SI base units in this dictionary, while density, velocity, acceleration, pressure, energy, power, viscosity, and heat-flux units are derived according to the BIPM SI conventions.

Let $\operatorname{Sym}(3)=\{D\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:D^T=D\}$, let $I$ be the $3\times3$ identity matrix, and define
$$\operatorname{SO}(3)=\{Q\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:Q^TQ=I,\ \det Q=1\}.$$
An orthogonal matrix is one with $Q^TQ=I$; define $O(3)$ by this condition without the determinant restriction. For $D\in\operatorname{Sym}(3)$ set $\operatorname{tr}D=\sum_{i=1}^3D_{ii}$. Suppose $L:\operatorname{Sym}(3)\to\operatorname{Sym}(3)$ is real-linear, meaning $L(aD+bE)=aL(D)+bL(E)$ for all $a,b\in\mathbb R$ and $D,E\in\operatorname{Sym}(3)$, and satisfies
$$L(QDQ^T)=QL(D)Q^T\qquad(Q\in\operatorname{SO}(3),\ D\in\operatorname{Sym}(3)).$$
Then there are unique $\lambda,\mu\in\mathbb R$ such that
$$L(D)=2\mu D+\lambda(\operatorname{tr}D)I\qquad(D\in\operatorname{Sym}(3)).$$
Conversely, each map of this form is real-linear and satisfies the displayed equivariance. Linearity and rotational equivariance are hypotheses of this mathematical classification; it does not assert that a material response is linear or isotropic.

Let $I\subset\mathbb R$ be an open time interval. Use the Cartesian inertial-chart convention of the adopted continuum balances on Newtonian spacetime $I\times E$: $E$ is an oriented Euclidean affine three-space, and the event-coordinate map is $(t,X)\mapsto(t,x_t(X))$ with $x_t(X)=b(X)+tw$, where $b:E\to\mathbb R^3$ is an orientation-preserving affine isometry and $w\in\mathbb R^3$ is constant. Time is absolute and measured in seconds, spatial coordinates in metres, and $w$ in metres per second. All derivatives below use this fixed chart. Let $\Omega\subset I\times\mathbb R^3$ be open. A smooth constant-density incompressible Newtonian branch has a constant $\rho_0>0$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, a constant dynamic shear viscosity $\mu\ge0$ in $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$, a velocity field $u\in C^2(\Omega,\mathbb R^3)$ measured in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, and a pressure multiplier $p\in C^1(\Omega,\mathbb R)$ measured in $\mathrm{Pa}$. Define $L_{ij}=\partial_{x_j}u_i$, $D=(L+L^T)/2$, and $D_tu=\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u$. The branch is specified by
$$ \rho=\rho_0,\qquad \operatorname{div}u=0,\qquad \sigma=-pI_3+2\mu D,\qquad \rho_0D_tu=\operatorname{div}\sigma, $$
where $(\operatorname{div}\sigma)_i=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}\sigma_{ij}$. Equivalently, for constant $\mu$, its momentum equation is
$$ \rho_0D_tu+\nabla p=\mu\Delta u,\qquad \Delta u_i=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_jx_j}u_i. $$
Indeed, $\operatorname{div}(2\mu D)=\mu\Delta u+\mu\nabla(\operatorname{div}u)=\mu\Delta u$. This is the incompressible specialization of the adopted Newtonian closure: $\theta=\operatorname{div}u=0$ implies $D_0=D$, so the bulk-viscosity and Fourier-flux terms do not enter this mechanical equation. The pressure is a constraint multiplier and is not identified with a compressible equation-of-state pressure. Define the kinematic viscosity $\nu=\mu/\rho_0$, in $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$. Boundary and initial data are not part of this definition, and the item asserts no solution existence.

Adopt specified scalar state laws $\mu,\zeta:\mathcal S\to[0,\infty)$ and a specified conductivity matrix law $K:\mathcal S\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$, with
$$ x^T\operatorname{sym}K(\xi)x\ge0\quad(x\in\mathbb R^3),\qquad \operatorname{sym}K:=(K+K^T)/2. $$
The conductivity law is tensor-valued and may be anisotropic; no restriction $K=kI_3$ is imposed. Define $\operatorname{Sym}(3):=\{D\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:D^T=D\}$ and $\operatorname{SO}(3):=\{Q\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:Q^TQ=I_3,\ \det Q=1\}$. Here $E$ is a three-dimensional oriented Euclidean affine space: its translation vectors form an oriented Euclidean vector space, but no origin in $E$ is distinguished. A **Cartesian inertial chart** is an event-coordinate map $(t,X)\mapsto(t,x_t(X))$, where $b:E\to\mathbb R^3$ is an orientation-preserving affine isometry, $w\in\mathbb R^3$ is constant, and $x_t(X)=b(X)+tw$ for $t\in I$. The affine map $b$ is auxiliary data defined on $E$, so this formula requires no evaluation at time $0$ when $0\notin I$. Each fixed-time spatial map is an orientation-preserving affine isometry with fixed spatial orientation; the spatial origin has constant velocity. Spatial coordinates are measured in metres and $w$ in metres per second. A chart may also use a translated absolute-time coordinate; at corresponding events the inertial-chart transformations are the ones displayed below. Write $\mathrm{SO}(3)=\{Q\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:Q^TQ=I_3,\det Q=1\}$. Inertial charts are related by

$$t^*=t+t_0,\qquad x^*=Qx+vt+a,$$

where $t_0$ is a constant time translation in seconds, $Q\in\mathrm{SO}(3)$ is constant, $v\in\mathbb R^3$ is a constant relative velocity in m s$^{-1}$, and $a\in\mathbb R^3$ is a constant spatial translation in metres. A **worldline** is a curve $t\mapsto(t,x(t))$ with $x\in C^2(I,\mathbb R^3)$, parameterized by absolute time; this model imposes no relativistic speed or causal condition. A **rigid observer change** is the more general coordinate change $t^*=t,\ x^*=Q(t)x+c(t)$, with $Q\in C^2(I,\mathrm{SO}(3))$ and $c\in C^2(I,\mathbb R^3)$ in metres; it is not called inertial unless $Q$ is constant and $c$ is affine in time. A frame here means an adapted Cartesian chart, not an observer congruence or a basis field.

For the initial-chart material-motion convention below, require $0\in I$. Let $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded open reference body whose boundary is locally the graph of a $C^1$ function, with $B$ lying on one side of each such graph. Identify the reference coordinates with the chosen initial Cartesian chart, and let $U$ be an open neighborhood of $\overline B$. A **material motion** is a map $\chi\in C^2(I\times U,\mathbb R^3)$ such that each $\chi_t=\chi(t,\cdot)$ is a bijection from $U$ onto an open image, has a $C^2$ inverse, and has positive Jacobian determinant; in the initial chart set $\chi(0,a)=a$. The label $a\in U$ and position $x=\chi(t,a)$ are measured in metres. Write

$$F(t,a)=D_a\chi(t,a),\qquad J(t,a)=\det F(t,a)>0,\qquad A(t,x)=\chi_t^{-1}(x),\qquad \Omega_t=\chi_t(B).$$

Here $F$ and $J$ are dimensionless and $A$ has units metres. The material map $\chi$ describes motion of the medium; it is not a change of observer or frame. The Eulerian velocity is the vector field defined by $u(t,\chi(t,a))=\partial_t\chi(t,a)$, measured in m s$^{-1}$. For a differentiable scalar or component field $f$, its material derivative is $D_tf=\partial_tf+u\cdot\nabla f$. $$\operatorname{curl}u=(\partial_yu_z-\partial_zu_y,\ \partial_zu_x-\partial_xu_z,\ \partial_xu_y-\partial_yu_x),$$

also in s$^{-1}$. In this library, a motion is **material-incompressible** on a region when $\operatorname{div}u=0$ there; **spatially homogeneous density** means $\nabla\rho=0$ there. These are distinct conditions. A **pathline** is a $C^1$ curve $X$ on an interval where the field is defined and the solution exists, satisfying $dX/dt=u(t,X(t))$. A **streamline at time $t_0$** is a $C^1$ integral curve satisfying $dX/ds=u(t_0,X(s))$ for a frozen $t_0$, with curve parameter $s$ measured in seconds. These are different constructions for an unsteady field.

A spatial vector is an element of the Euclidean translation space; its components rotate by $Q$ under a rigid observer change. A spatial second-order tensor is a linear map from that vector space to itself, represented by a $3\times3$ matrix in a Cartesian orthonormal basis; it transforms as $S^*=QSQ^T$. A tensor-valued constitutive response is **objective** when its values at corresponding events satisfy this transformation rule for every $C^2$ rigid observer change. On each swept material region, require $\rho,u,e,T,s,q,\sigma\in C^1$ and $b,r\in C^0$, with $\rho>0$ and $T>0$; the motion has the regularity and positive Jacobian in the preceding definition. A material subregion is $\chi_t(V)$ for a nonempty bounded open set $V\Subset B$ whose boundary is locally, after a rigid coordinate change, a $C^1$ graph with $V$ on one side; its boundary moves with the material velocity. All volume integrals here use the componentwise Riemann integral by zero extension to a containing closed rectangle. A bounded set is Jordan measurable when its indicator has such a Riemann integral; a set has content zero when, for every positive $\varepsilon$, it has a finite cover by axis-parallel boxes whose total volume is less than $\varepsilon$, where box volume is the product of side lengths. For each permitted $V$ and its image $\chi_t(V)$, their compact closures are Jordan measurable and their boundaries have content zero. For every continuous scalar integrand $f$ on a neighborhood of $\chi_t(\overline V)$, $\int_{\chi_t(V)}f\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(\overline V)}f\,dx$; the analogous equality is used on $V$ and $\overline V$. Vector and tensor integrals are taken componentwise. These are the earlier $C^1$-region integral conventions, so the displayed balances over open material regions have the same meaning as their compact-closure transport formulas. For each current boundary $S=\partial\chi_t(V)$, surface integration is the finite-chart Riemann convention: for any continuous scalar $f$ on $S$, choose regular $C^1$ graph charts $X_j:U_j\subset\mathbb R^2\to S\cap O_j$ and a finite nonnegative subordinate smooth ambient partition $\chi_j$ with compact support in the chart neighborhoods and sum one on $S$, and put $\int_S f\,dS=\sum_j\int_{U_j}(\chi_j f)(X_j(y))\sqrt{\det(DX_j(y)^TDX_j(y))}\,dy$. Each parameter integrand is extended by zero outside $U_j$. These integrals are finite and independent of charts and partition; in graph coordinates the density is $\sqrt{1+|Dh|^2}$. The unit normal is the continuous outward normal, and vector surface integrals are componentwise. Thus all traction, work, heat and entropy fluxes below use the same boundary-area convention. When a consuming mathematical theorem separately assumes Countable Choice, these continuous-field surface integrals also agree with its finite-chart Lebesgue surface integrals with the same Gram density; that conditional mathematical agreement adds no choice assumption to this physical postulate. The continuum approximation, its empirical regime, and the following balance laws are physical assumptions of this model, not deductions from the mathematical definition of a motion or from molecular mechanics.

Assume there are no mass sources and no diffusion relative to $u$. Adopt a positive reference mass density $\rho_0$, a positive current density $\rho$, a body-acceleration field $b$, a contact traction $t(t,x,n)=\sigma(t,x)n$ depending only on the local outward unit normal $n$, a $C^1$ Cauchy stress field $\sigma$, specific internal energy $e$, positive temperature $T$, specific entropy $s$, heat-flux vector $q$, and specific heat supply $r$, with the types and SI units fixed in the preceding definition. Contact traction and volume-force densities are continuous and locally bounded on the smooth material regions under consideration. There are no surface couples or intrinsic spin angular momentum; a micropolar or couple-stress model is outside this postulate.

For every such material subregion, adopt conservation of mass,

$$\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho(t,x)\,dx=\int_V\rho_0(a)\,da.$$

In the same inertial chart, adopt the balances of linear and angular momentum,

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho u\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho b\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}t(t,x,n)\,dS,$$

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}x\times(\rho u)\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}x\times(\rho b)\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}x\times t(t,x,n)\,dS.$$

Adopt the total-energy balance and entropy inequality

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho\left(e+\frac{|u|^2}{2}\right)\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho b\cdot u\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}t(t,x,n)\cdot u\,dS-\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}q\cdot n\,dS+\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho r\,dx,$$

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho s\,dx\ge-\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}\frac{q}{T}\cdot n\,dS+\int_{\chi_t(V)}\frac{\rho r}{T}\,dx.$$

The entropy flux uses the local material temperature at the heat-transfer point. A reservoir at a different temperature, a singular surface force, a shock, vacuum, or a weak solution requires a separately stated model and is not covered here. The postulate reports no experiment and asserts no measurement or universal claim that nature obeys these assumptions.

Use a smooth single-component, nonpolar fluid branch in a Cartesian inertial frame. Let $\mathcal U\subset(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R$ be an open state domain with coordinates $v$ and $s$, where $v$ is specific volume and $s$ is specific entropy. Adopt a specific internal-energy function $e:\mathcal U\to\mathbb R$ of class $C^2$, meaning that its coordinate partial derivatives through total order two exist and are continuous. At a state $(v,s)$, define the temperature and thermodynamic pressure by
$$ T(v,s)=\frac{\partial e}{\partial s}(v,s),\qquad p(v,s)=-\frac{\partial e}{\partial v}(v,s),\qquad \rho=\frac1v, $$
where each partial derivative holds the other state coordinate fixed. Assume the local material states lie in $\mathcal U$ and $T>0$. Local equilibrium here means that the fields $e,T,p$ at each event are assigned by these state functions of the local $v,s$.

In the physical SI interpretation, $v$ is in $\mathrm{m^3\,kg^{-1}}$, $s$ in $\mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$, $e$ in $\mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}}$, $T$ in $\mathrm K$, $p$ in $\mathrm{Pa}$, and $\rho$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$. Positivity of $e_{ss}$, global invertibility of $s\mapsto T$, convexity, and the dynamical entropy inequality are separate assumptions or postulates; none follows from this local equilibrium adoption. This closure is an additional physical model choice, not a consequence of global equilibrium thermodynamics.

Use a Cartesian inertial frame in Newtonian spacetime. At an event let $u$ be the fluid velocity, $T>0$ its temperature, $\rho>0$ its mass density, and $\xi=(\rho,T)$ its local state in a specified open set $\mathcal S\subset(0,\infty)^2$. The velocity gradient has components $L_{ij}=\partial_{x_j}u_i$; define the symmetric rate matrix $D=(L+L^T)/2$, its trace $\theta=\operatorname{tr}D$, and its trace-free part $D_0=D-\theta I_3/3$, where $I_3$ is the $3\times3$ identity matrix. For $A,B\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}$, use the Frobenius contraction $A:B=\sum_{i,j=1}^3A_{ij}B_{ij}$.

Adopt specified scalar state laws $\mu,\zeta:\mathcal S\to[0,\infty)$ and a specified conductivity matrix law $K:\mathcal S\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$, with
$$ x^T\operatorname{sym}K(\xi)x\ge0\quad(x\in\mathbb R^3),\qquad \operatorname{sym}K:=(K+K^T)/2. $$
The conductivity law is tensor-valued and may be anisotropic; no restriction $K=kI_3$ is imposed. Define $\operatorname{Sym}(3):=\{D\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:D^T=D\}$ and $\operatorname{SO}(3):=\{Q\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:Q^TQ=I_3,\ \det Q=1\}$. At a fixed state, let $\mathcal A_\xi:\operatorname{Sym}(3)\to\operatorname{Sym}(3)$ assign the viscous stress to the symmetric rate matrix. Assume it is real-linear, meaning $\mathcal A_\xi(aD+bE)=a\mathcal A_\xi(D)+b\mathcal A_\xi(E)$ for all $a,b\in\mathbb R$ and $D,E\in\operatorname{Sym}(3)$, and equivariant in the sense $\mathcal A_\xi(QDQ^T)=Q\mathcal A_\xi(D)Q^T$ for every $Q\in\operatorname{SO}(3)$. Adopt
$$ \tau=\mathcal A_\xi(D)=2\mu(\xi)D_0+\zeta(\xi)\theta I_3,\qquad \sigma=-pI_3+\tau,\qquad q=-K(\xi)\nabla T. $$
Here $p$ is the scalar pressure field in the tension-positive convention: the traction on an outward unit normal $n$ is $\sigma n$. Under a rigid observer rotation $Q\in\operatorname{SO}(3)$, tensor fields transform by $S^*=QSQ^T$; $\mu,\zeta$ are scalar state functions and $K^*=QKQ^T$. The viscous response is isotropic in this proper-rotation sense, while the conductivity tensor transforms covariantly and may be anisotropic. The mathematical linear-isotropic classification identifies this stress form from the stated domain, codomain, linearity and equivariance hypotheses; it does not establish that any material adopts them.

In SI units, $D,\theta,D_0$ are in $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, $\mu,\zeta$ in $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$, $K$ in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$, $q$ in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$, and $\sigma,\tau,p$ in $\mathrm{Pa}$. If the same stress is written $2\mu D+\lambda\theta I_3$, then $\lambda=\zeta-2\mu/3$; no nonnegativity of $\lambda$ is assumed. These specified constitutive functions are adopted model inputs, not measured coefficient values or consequences of balance laws.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$: every sequence $(X_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ of nonempty sets has a function $f$ with $f(n)\in X_n$ for every $n$. Let $U\subset(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R$ be open and let $e:U\to\mathbb R$ have continuous total derivatives through order two. For $(v,s)\in U$, $v$ is the specific-volume coordinate, $s$ the specific-entropy coordinate, and $e(v,s)$ the specific-energy value; set $T=e_s(v,s)$ and $p=-e_v(v,s)$, with each state partial derivative holding the other coordinate fixed.

Let $I\subset\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval. Let $B\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty bounded open set with $C^1$ boundary, meaning that near every boundary point it is the graph of a continuously differentiable function after a rigid coordinate change. Let $N\subset\mathbb R^3$ be open with $\overline B\subset N$, and let $\chi\in C^2(I\times N,\mathbb R^3)$, where $C^r$ means that all coordinate partial derivatives through total order $r$ exist and are continuous. For each $t\in I$, assume $\chi_t(a):=\chi(t,a)$ is a bijection from $N$ onto an open set with a $C^2$ inverse and $\det D_a\chi(t,a)>0$. Define $\Omega_t:=\chi_t(B)$, $\Omega:=\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\Omega_t\}$, and $u(t,x):=\partial_t\chi(t,\chi_t^{-1}(x))$; this swept set $\Omega$ is open. For a scalar or vector field $f$ on $\Omega$, set $D_tf:=\partial_tf+\sum_{j=1}^3u_j\partial_{x_j}f$ componentwise. For each nonempty bounded open $C^1$ subdomain $V$ with $\overline V\subset B$, set $P_t:=\chi_t(V)$; here a $C^1$ domain is locally on one side of a $C^1$ boundary graph.

Let $\rho,v,s,T,p,q,r,b$ be fields on $\Omega$ with continuous first partial derivatives, with $\rho>0$, $(v,s)\in U$, $v=1/\rho$, $T=e_s(v,s)>0$, and $p=-e_v(v,s)$. Let $e$ on $\Omega$ denote the composition $e(v,s)$. Let $\sigma$ be a continuously differentiable $3\times3$ stress matrix field, let $\tau$ be a continuously differentiable $3\times3$ matrix field, and suppose $\sigma=-pI+\tau$, where $I$ is the $3\times3$ identity. For a scalar field $h$, define $(\nabla h)_i:=\partial_{x_i}h$; define $L:=\nabla u$ by $L_{ij}:=\partial_{x_j}u_i$, $D:=(L+L^T)/2$, and $\theta:=\operatorname{tr}D=\sum_{i=1}^3\partial_{x_i}u_i$. Define $A:B:=\sum_{i,j=1}^3A_{ij}B_{ij}$ for matrices, $\operatorname{div}q:=\sum_i\partial_{x_i}q_i$, and $\operatorname{div}(q/T)$ componentwise. Put $a_m:=\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u$, $k:=|u|^2/2$, and $E:=e+k$. The fields $u,q,b$ are vector-valued and $r$ is scalar-valued.

Assume there is a contact traction $t_c(t,y,n)\in\mathbb R^3$ depending on a surface only through its point $y$ and outward unit normal $n\in S^2$, continuous in $(y,n)$ and uniformly bounded near each point. Assume its local force balance $\int_{\partial P}t_c(t,y,\nu_P(y))\,dS_y+\int_P\rho(t,y)(b(t,y)-a_m(t,y))\,dy=0$ for every nonempty bounded open $C^1$ subdomain $P$ whose closure is compactly contained in $\Omega_t$. Surface integrals use Euclidean surface measure with chart area density $\sqrt{\det(DX^TDX)}$. Suppose the unique Cauchy stress supplied by this contact balance satisfies $t_c(t,y,n)=\sigma(t,y)n$ and has the stated $C^1$ regularity; the contact result alone does not imply that regularity.

Assume the pointwise continuity equation $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(\rho u)=0$ and, for every such material subdomain $V$ and every $t\in I$, the integral balances
$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{P_t}\rho u\,dx=\int_{P_t}\rho b\,dx+\int_{\partial P_t}\sigma\nu\,dS,$$
$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{P_t}x\times(\rho u)\,dx=\int_{P_t}x\times(\rho b)\,dx+\int_{\partial P_t}x\times(\sigma\nu)\,dS,$$
$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{P_t}\rho E\,dx=\int_{P_t}\rho b\cdot u\,dx+\int_{\partial P_t}(\sigma\nu)\cdot u\,dS-\int_{\partial P_t}q\cdot\nu\,dS+\int_{P_t}\rho r\,dx,$$
where $\nu$ is the outward unit normal, $\times$ is the ordinary vector cross product, and all fields are continuous up to the swept closures. The angular-momentum balance gives $\sigma=\sigma^T$, and the local internal-energy equation supplied by these hypotheses is $\rho D_te=\sigma:D-\operatorname{div}q+\rho r$. Define the entropy residual $\mathcal G:=\rho D_ts+\operatorname{div}(q/T)-\rho r/T$. Then
$$\mathcal G=\frac{\tau:D}{T}-\frac{q\cdot\nabla T}{T^2}.$$
At any state with $e_{ss}>0$, a unique local $C^1$ branch $s(v,T)$ satisfies $e_s(v,s(v,T))=T$; the local Helmholtz function $a(v,T):=e(v,s(v,T))-Ts(v,T)$ then satisfies $a_T=-s$ and $a_v=-p$. The entropy identity does not assert $\mathcal G\ge0$ and makes no empirical claim. In the physical SI interpretation, $\rho$ is in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, $u$ in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $b$ in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, $v$ in $\mathrm{m^3\,kg^{-1}}$, $e,k,E$ in $\mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}}$, $s$ in $\mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$, $T$ in $\mathrm K$, $p,\sigma,\tau,t_c$ in $\mathrm{Pa}$, $q$ in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$, and $r$ in $\mathrm{W\,kg^{-1}}$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$: every sequence of nonempty sets admits a choice function. At a fixed state, let $\mu,\lambda\in\mathbb R$, $K\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}$, $T>0$, $g\in\mathbb R^3$, and let $D\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ be symmetric. Put
$$\theta:=\operatorname{tr}D=\sum_{i=1}^3D_{ii},\qquad D_0:=D-\frac{\theta}{3}I,\qquad \zeta:=\lambda+\frac{2\mu}{3},\qquad \operatorname{sym}K:=\frac{K+K^T}{2},$$
where $I$ is the $3\times3$ identity and $|D_0|^2:=\sum_{i,j=1}^3(D_0)_{ij}^2$. Use the Newtonian stress expression $\tau:=2\mu D+\lambda\theta I$ and the Fourier flux expression $q:=-Kg$, and define the quadratic residual
$$\mathcal Q(D,g,T):=\frac{\tau:D}{T}-\frac{q\cdot g}{T^2}, \qquad \tau:D:=\sum_{i,j=1}^3\tau_{ij}D_{ij}.$$
Here $g$ represents an independently varied temperature-gradient value. The coefficient equivalence is an algebraic statement about $\mathcal Q$; its interpretation as an entropy residual is conditional on the local state and balance hypotheses of the Gibbs identity.
For these definitions the exact algebraic decomposition is
$$\mathcal Q(D,g,T)=\frac{2\mu|D_0|^2+\zeta\theta^2}{T}+\frac{g^T(\operatorname{sym}K)g}{T^2}.$$
Then $\mathcal Q(D,g,T)\ge0$ for every symmetric $D$, every $g\in\mathbb R^3$, and every $T>0$ if and only if
$$\mu\ge0,\qquad \zeta\ge0,\qquad x^T(\operatorname{sym}K)x\ge0\quad\text{for every }x\in\mathbb R^3.$$
In particular, $\lambda$ need not be nonnegative: if $\mu>0$ and $\zeta=0$, then $\lambda=-2\mu/3$ and the coefficient conditions still hold when $\operatorname{sym}K$ is positive semidefinite. This is an algebraic coefficient test for the conditional entropy residual; it neither derives a constitutive law nor assigns material coefficients. In the physical SI interpretation, $\mu,\lambda,\zeta$ have units $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$, $D$ has units $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, $K$ has units $\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$, $g$ has units $\mathrm{K\,m^{-1}}$, and $T$ has units $\mathrm K$.

Here $\operatorname{div}u=\sum_{i=1}^3\partial_{x_i}u_i$, $
abla$ is the spatial gradient, and $D_tu=\partial_tu+(u\cdot
abla)u$ is the material acceleration. The constitutive stress is $\sigma=-P(ho)I_3$ under the tension-positive traction convention. Thus “barotropic” means that pressure is a specified function of density alone, and “Euler” here means that the viscous stress is absent. No sign of $P'(ho)$ is built into the definition; a positive acoustic response is a separate hypothesis where used. In SI interpretation, $ho$ is in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, $u$ in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $P$ in $\mathrm{Pa}$, and $P'(ho)$ in $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}$. Use a smooth single-component, nonpolar fluid branch in a Cartesian inertial frame. Let $\mathcal U\subset(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R$ be an open state domain with coordinates $v$ and $s$, where $v$ is specific volume and $s$ is specific entropy. Adopt a specific internal-energy function $e:\mathcal U\to\mathbb R$ of class $C^2$, meaning that its coordinate partial derivatives through total order two exist and are continuous. At a state $(v,s)$, define the temperature and thermodynamic pressure by
$$ T(v,s)=\frac{\partial e}{\partial s}(v,s),\qquad p(v,s)=-\frac{\partial e}{\partial v}(v,s),\qquad \rho=\frac1v, $$
where each partial derivative holds the other state coordinate fixed. Assume the local material states lie in $\mathcal U$ and $T>0$. Local equilibrium here means that the fields $e,T,p$ at each event are assigned by these state functions of the local $v,s$.

In the physical SI interpretation, $v$ is in $\mathrm{m^3\,kg^{-1}}$, $s$ in $\mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$, $e$ in $\mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}}$, $T$ in $\mathrm K$, $p$ in $\mathrm{Pa}$, and $\rho$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$. Positivity of $e_{ss}$, global invertibility of $s\mapsto T$, convexity, and the dynamical entropy inequality are separate assumptions or postulates; none follows from this local equilibrium adoption. This closure is an additional physical model choice, not a consequence of global equilibrium thermodynamics.

Let $U\subset(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R$ be open and let $e:U\to\mathbb R$ have continuous total derivatives through order two. Fix $(v_b,s_b)\in U$ with $T_b=e_s(v_b,s_b)>0$ and $e_{ss}(v_b,s_b)>0$, set $\rho_b=1/v_b$ and $p=-e_v$, and use the local chart $s=s(v,T)$ from the unique branch satisfying $e_s(v,s(v,T))=T$. Define
$$c_v:=\left.\frac{\partial}{\partial T}e(v,s(v,T))\right|_{v=v_b,T=T_b}, \qquad c_s^2:=v_b^2 e_{vv}(v_b,s_b).$$
Because $U$ is open, choose an open interval $J_\rho\subset(0,\infty)$ containing $\rho_b$ such that $(1/\rho,s_b)\in U$ for every $\rho\in J_\rho$, and define $P:J_\rho\to\mathbb R$ by $P(\rho):=p(1/\rho,s_b)=-e_v(1/\rho,s_b)$. Then $P\in C^1(J_\rho)$ and the chain rule gives $P'(\rho_b)=v_b^2e_{vv}(v_b,s_b)=c_s^2$. This is the local isentropic pressure-response coefficient; its sign is not assumed.

Let $I\subset\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open time interval. On $I\times\mathbb R^3$, let $\rho:I\times\mathbb R^3\to J_\rho$ and $u:I\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ have continuous partial derivatives through order two. Use the Euclidean dot product $x\cdot y:=\sum_{i=1}^3x_i y_i$ and norm $|x|:=\sqrt{x\cdot x}$ on $\mathbb R^3$. Use $\nabla h=(\partial_{x_i}h)_{i=1}^3$, $\operatorname{div}u=\sum_{i=1}^3\partial_{x_i}u_i$, and $(u\cdot\nabla)u_i=\sum_{j=1}^3u_j\partial_{x_j}u_i$. Consider the mathematical barotropic system
$$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(\rho u)=0,\qquad \rho\bigl(\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u\bigr)+\nabla P(\rho)=0.$$
Here $\Delta r:=\sum_{i=1}^3\partial_{x_i x_i}r$. For $r:I\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ and $w:I\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ with continuous partial derivatives through order two, the pointwise first variation about $(\rho_b,0)$ is defined by differentiating at $\varepsilon=0$ after substituting $\rho=\rho_b+\varepsilon r$ and $u=\varepsilon w$, with $\varepsilon$ sufficiently close to zero locally at each point so the perturbed density lies in $J_\rho$. It is
$$r_t+\rho_b\operatorname{div}w=0,\qquad \rho_b w_t+c_s^2\nabla r=0, \qquad r_{tt}=c_s^2\Delta r.$$
If $c_s^2>0$, then with $c_s=\sqrt{c_s^2}$, for every nonzero $k\in\mathbb R^3$ and every $A\in\mathbb R$ the following are plane-wave solutions:
$$r=A\cos(k\cdot x-\omega t),\qquad w=\frac{\omega A}{\rho_b|k|^2}k\cos(k\cdot x-\omega t),\qquad \omega=c_s|k|.$$
If $c_s^2<0$, then for every nonzero $k\in\mathbb R^3$ and every $A\in\mathbb R$, set $a=\sqrt{-c_s^2}|k|>0$. The fields
$$r=Ae^{at}\cos(k\cdot x),\qquad w=-\frac{aA}{\rho_b|k|^2}k e^{at}\sin(k\cdot x)$$
solve the same linearized system and have exponential time factor $e^{at}$; for $A\ne0$, their amplitudes grow exponentially. These are exact statements about the linearized mathematical system; they provide no finite-amplitude error or lifespan estimate and make no empirical claim about a material.

derivations.claim: Since $P(\rho)=p(1/\rho,s_b)$ and $p=-e_v$, the chain rule at fixed $s_b$ gives $P'(\rho_b)=p_v(v_b,s_b)(-1/\rho_b^2)=(-e_{vv})(-v_b^2)=v_b^2e_{vv}$. This is $c_s^2$ by definition.

Substitute $\rho_\varepsilon=\rho_b+\varepsilon\delta\rho$ and $u_\varepsilon=\varepsilon w$ into the model equations from [L1]. The order-$\varepsilon$ continuity term is $\partial_t\delta\rho+\rho_b\operatorname{div}w$. The convective term in momentum is order $\varepsilon^2$, while differentiability of $P$ gives $\nabla P(\rho_\varepsilon)=\varepsilon P'(\rho_b)\nabla\delta\rho+o(\varepsilon)$. Dividing by $\varepsilon$ and taking the derivative at zero yields the stated first-variation system.

Differentiate the first equation of the first-variation system in time. Take the divergence of the second equation; because $\rho_b$ and $P'(\rho_b)=c_s^2$ are constant, substitution gives $\partial_{tt}\delta\rho=c_s^2\Delta\delta\rho$.

Suppose $c_s^2>0$, take $k\ne0$, and put $\omega=c_s|k|$. For the stated fields, $\partial_t\delta\rho=\omega A\sin(k\cdot x-\omega t)$, $\nabla\delta\rho=-Ak\sin(k\cdot x-\omega t)$, $\operatorname{div}w=-\omega A\sin(k\cdot x-\omega t)/\rho_b$, and $\partial_tw=\omega^2Ak\sin(k\cdot x-\omega t)/(\rho_b|k|^2)$. The continuity equation follows from the first and third expressions; the momentum equation follows from $\omega^2=c_s^2|k|^2$.

Let $I\subset\mathbb R$ be an open time interval. Use the Cartesian inertial-chart convention of the adopted continuum balances on Newtonian spacetime $I\times E$: $E$ is an oriented Euclidean affine three-space, and the event-coordinate map is $(t,X)\mapsto(t,x_t(X))$ with $x_t(X)=b(X)+tw$, where $b:E\to\mathbb R^3$ is an orientation-preserving affine isometry and $w\in\mathbb R^3$ is constant. Time is absolute and measured in seconds, spatial coordinates in metres, and $w$ in metres per second. All derivatives below use this fixed chart. Let $\Omega\subset I\times\mathbb R^3$ be open. A smooth constant-density incompressible Newtonian branch has a constant $\rho_0>0$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, a constant dynamic shear viscosity $\mu\ge0$ in $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$, a velocity field $u\in C^2(\Omega,\mathbb R^3)$ measured in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, and a pressure multiplier $p\in C^1(\Omega,\mathbb R)$ measured in $\mathrm{Pa}$. Define $L_{ij}=\partial_{x_j}u_i$, $D=(L+L^T)/2$, and $D_tu=\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u$. The branch is specified by
$$ \rho=\rho_0,\qquad \operatorname{div}u=0,\qquad \sigma=-pI_3+2\mu D,\qquad \rho_0D_tu=\operatorname{div}\sigma, $$
where $(\operatorname{div}\sigma)_i=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}\sigma_{ij}$. Equivalently, for constant $\mu$, its momentum equation is
$$ \rho_0D_tu+\nabla p=\mu\Delta u,\qquad \Delta u_i=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_jx_j}u_i. $$
Indeed, $\operatorname{div}(2\mu D)=\mu\Delta u+\mu\nabla(\operatorname{div}u)=\mu\Delta u$. This is the incompressible specialization of the adopted Newtonian closure: $\theta=\operatorname{div}u=0$ implies $D_0=D$, so the bulk-viscosity and Fourier-flux terms do not enter this mechanical equation. The pressure is a constraint multiplier and is not identified with a compressible equation-of-state pressure. Define the kinematic viscosity $\nu=\mu/\rho_0$, in $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$. Boundary and initial data are not part of this definition, and the item asserts no solution existence.

Let $V\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded open set whose boundary is locally, after a rigid coordinate change, the graph of a $C^1$ function, with $V$ lying locally on one side of that graph. Let $U\subset\mathbb R^3$ be open with $\overline V\subset U$. Let $\phi:U\to\phi(U)$ be a bijection onto an open image with $\phi$ and $\phi^{-1}$ both $C^1$, and let $f:\phi(U)\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. A bounded set is Jordan measurable when its indicator is Riemann integrable by the zero-extension convention; a set has content zero when it has finite cube covers of arbitrarily small total volume. Then $V$ and $\phi(V)$ are bounded open sets with locally $C^1$ graph boundaries, their compact closures are Jordan measurable, $\partial V$ and $\phi(\partial V)$ have content zero, and

$$\int_{\phi(V)}f(x)\,dx=\int_{\phi(\overline V)}f(x)\,dx.$$

Thus a balance integral over an open $C^1$ material region agrees with the compact-Jordan integral on its closure after a $C^1$ diffeomorphic motion.

Let $A\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $B\subseteq\mathbb R^q$ be nondegenerate closed rectangles, and let $f:A\times B\to\mathbb R$ be Riemann integrable. Then the four lower and upper section-integral functions of [[def-sections-and-iterated-riemann-integrals]] are Riemann integrable and
$$\int_A\ell_B=\int_Au_B=\int_{A\times B}f=\int_B\ell_A=\int_Bu_A.$$

If the $B$-sections are integrable outside a content-zero set $N\subseteq A$, every bounded exceptionally completed function $h$ with $h(x)=\int_Bf_x$ for $x\notin N$ is integrable and
$$\int_{A\times B}f=\int_Ah.$$
The same assertion holds with the coordinate blocks exchanged. In particular, when every section in an order is integrable, the ordinary iterated integral in that order exists and equals the multiple integral. The theorem does not assert that every section of an integrable function is integrable.

Let $a<b$. Suppose $G:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$. If $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is Riemann integrable and

$$f(x)=G'(x)\qquad(a<x<b),$$

then

$$\int_a^b f=G(b)-G(a).$$

No derivative of $G$ at either endpoint is assumed, and the two endpoint values assigned to the integrable extension $f$ do not enter the conclusion.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ (Continuity of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point of $A$ and on $A$: the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, its agreement with $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ at a limit point, and continuity at an isolated point, Intervals of $\mathbb{R}$: the nine order-convex forms, nondegeneracy, and length) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $(X,d_X)$ be a compact metric space (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space), let
$(Y,d_Y)$ be any metric space (Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric) and let $f : X \to Y$ be
continuous (Continuity of a map between metric spaces, at a point and globally, in the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ form). Then $f$ is uniformly continuous
(Uniform continuity of a map of metric spaces: one $\delta$ serving every point).

No choice principle is used: the cover built below is cut out by a property, and
the Lebesgue number lemma it is fed to is itself choice free
(Every open cover of a compact metric space has a Lebesgue number: a $\delta > 0$ such that every nonempty subset of diameter less than $\delta$ lies inside a single member of the cover).

$f,g:Q\to\mathbb R$ and scalars $\alpha,\beta$, the function
$\alpha f+\beta g$ is integrable and its integral is
$\alpha\int_Qf+\beta\int_Qg$. If $f\le g$, then
$\int_Qf\le\int_Qg$. Also $|f|$ is integrable and
$|\int_Qf|\le\int_Q|f|$. If $a_r<c<b_r$, cutting $Q$ at the coordinate

The pointwise model equation in [A1] holds on the same fixed spatial region used in the energy integral (or on its periodic lift). Dot $\rho_0D_tu=\operatorname{div}\sigma$ with $u$. The component product rule gives $u_i\partial_{x_j}\sigma_{ij}=\partial_{x_j}(\sigma_{ij}u_i)-\sigma_{ij}\partial_{x_j}u_i$, while $D_t(|u|^2/2)=u\cdot D_tu$. Since $\rho_0$ is constant and $\operatorname{div}u=0$, this yields
$$ \partial_t\left(\frac{\rho_0|u|^2}{2}\right) +\operatorname{div}\left(\frac{\rho_0|u|^2}{2}u-\sigma^Tu\right) =-\sigma:\nabla u. $$

Fix $t$ and put $e=\rho_0|u|^2/2$ and $F=eu-\sigma^Tu$. In the periodic case, [F2] integrates each $\partial_jF_j$ first in $x_j$; opposite endpoint values agree, so $\int_\Omega\operatorname{div}F=0$. In the bounded-domain case, $F$ is $C^1$ on a neighborhood of $\overline\Omega$ and vanishes on $\partial\Omega$. Here is a direct zero-flux argument requiring no additional choice axiom. Use a finite cubic mesh of side $h$ in a fixed containing box and let $P_h$ be the union of the closed mesh cubes contained in $\Omega$. Let $B_h$ be the union of mesh cubes at distance at most $4\sqrt3h$ from $\partial\Omega$. Since this compact boundary has content zero by [F1], $\operatorname{vol}(B_h)\to0$: for any finite open box cover of the boundary, all sufficiently small $B_h$ lie in that cover, and such covers have arbitrarily small total volume. Also $\Omega\setminus P_h\subseteq B_h$. Applying [F2] on each cube of $P_h$ and cancelling common faces expresses $\int_{P_h}\operatorname{div}F$ as the sum of the exposed face integrals. Each exposed face is within $2\sqrt3h$ of the boundary. The derivative of $F$ is bounded by a constant $M$ on a compact neighborhood of that boundary, so the segment mean-value estimate [F3] and $F|_{\partial\Omega}=0$ give $|F|\le2\sqrt3Mh$ on these faces for sufficiently small $h$. Their number is at most six times the number of cubes in $B_h$. Thus [F4] bounds the absolute sum of face integrals by $12\sqrt3M\operatorname{vol}(B_h)\to0$. Let $I\subset\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open time interval and $\Omega\subset I\times\mathbb R^3$ a nonempty open domain for the model fields. Let $e\in C^2(\mathcal U)$ be the local specific-energy relation on an open $\mathcal U\subset(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R$, with state coordinates $(v,s)$, $T=e_s$, and $p=-e_v$; each state partial derivative holds the other coordinate fixed. Fix $(v_b,s_b)\in\mathcal U$ with $T_b>0$ and $e_{ss}(v_b,s_b)>0$, set $\rho_b=1/v_b$, and take a barotropic pressure law $P\in C^1((0,\infty))$ that agrees with $p(1/\rho,s_b)$ on an open density interval $J_\rho\subset(0,\infty)$ containing $\rho_b$, with $(1/\rho,s_b)\in\mathcal U$ for every $\rho\in J_\rho$. This is the fixed-entropy restriction of the adopted local state relation. The smooth barotropic Euler model is linearized about the uniform rest state $(\rho,u)=(\rho_b,0)$. For $C^2$ perturbation fields $\delta\rho:I\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ and $w:I\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$, the first variation at $\varepsilon=0$ after $\rho=\rho_b+\varepsilon\delta\rho$, $u=\varepsilon w$ is
$$ \partial_t\delta\rho+\rho_b\operatorname{div}w=0,\qquad \rho_b\partial_tw+P'(\rho_b)\nabla\delta\rho=0,\qquad \partial_{tt}\delta\rho=c_s^2\Delta\delta\rho, \quad c_s^2=P'(\rho_b)=v_b^2e_{vv}(v_b,s_b). $$
The sign of $c_s^2$ is not assumed in the base model. If $c_s^2>0$, define $c_s=\sqrt{c_s^2}$. For every nonzero $k\in\mathbb R^3$, with $\omega=c_s|k|$, the fields
$$ \delta\rho=A\cos(k\cdot x-\omega t),\qquad w=\frac{\omega A}{\rho_b|k|^2}k\cos(k\cdot x-\omega t) $$
solve the first-variation system for every real amplitude $A$. They are exact solutions of the linearized equations, not finite-amplitude approximations with an automatic error or lifespan bound. No empirical value of $c_s$ is asserted.

In SI units, $t$ is in seconds, $x$ in metres, $\rho_b,\delta\rho,A$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, $u,w,c_s$ in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $k$ in $\mathrm{m^{-1}}$, $\omega$ in $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, and $c_s^2$ in $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}$.

derivations.claim: Differentiation of the chosen state relation gives $T_b>0$, $e_{ss}=C>0$, and $e_{vv}=-A<0$ at $(v_b,s_b)$. For $P(\rho)=p(1/\rho,s_b)$, the chain rule gives $P'(\rho_b)=v_b^2e_{vv}=-Av_b^2=c_s^2<0$.

The derivatives of the stated mode are $\partial_t\delta\rho=\alpha\delta\rho$, $\operatorname{div}w=-\alpha\delta\rho/\rho_b$, $\partial_tw=-\alpha^2a_0k e^{\alpha t}\sin(k\cdot x)/(\rho_b|k|^2)$, and $\nabla\delta\rho=-a_0k e^{\alpha t}\sin(k\cdot x)$. Therefore the continuity equation holds, and the momentum equation holds because $-\alpha^2/|k|^2-c_s^2=0$ by the definition of $\alpha$.

Since $\alpha>0$ and $k\cdot x$ cannot have both sine and cosine zero, at every fixed $x$ either $\delta\rho(t,x)$ or $w(t,x)$ has a nonzero coefficient multiplying $e^{\alpha t}$. Thus the pair is unbounded in time on $I=\mathbb R$, refuting the stated assertion. This smooth first-order solution concerns only the linearized mathematical system; it supplies no finite-amplitude solution or empirical material claim.
